title: Vak, the goddess who speaks
hookLine: a Rig Veda hymn where the goddess of speech says I, and why Hindus treat sacred sound with care
carry: Vak: the goddess is the power in every word

lines: NOT SUNG TO HER. SUNG BY HER.
VAK: THE GODDESS WHO IS SPEECH.
cards: I. A hymn can be sung to Agni, to Indra, to the dawn. This one in the Rig Veda is sung by someone.

The speaker is Vak, a goddess whose name means speech, and tradition names the hymn's seer as Vak, daughter of the sage Ambhrina: a woman's voice among the Rig Veda's seers. The whole hymn comes from her own mouth.
I move with the gods. I hold them up. I bend the bow.
I breathe out like the wind.

teach.h: I MOVE WITH THE GODS. I HOLD THEM UP.
teach.b: Here is some of the hymn, in paraphrase. I move with the Rudras and the Vasus, with the Adityas and all the gods. I hold up Mitra and Varuna, Indra and Agni.
I am the queen, the gatherer of treasures.

teach.h: THROUGH ME, THEY EAT, SEE, BREATHE.
teach.b: Through me eats the one who eats, the one who sees, breathes and hears. Without knowing it, they live in me. I bend the bow for Rudra.
I breathe out like the wind, taking hold of all the worlds. So great have I become. First, she holds the gods up, not the other way around.
Second, she's inside ordinary acts: eating, seeing, breathing, hearing, all done through her, without knowing it. Third, she reaches beyond the sky and the earth. Inside everything, and beyond it.
Here is the teaching. In Hindu thought, speech isn't only noise we make.
Vak is divine power, Shakti, as sound.

teach.h: WHY A MANTRA IS SAID WITH CARE.
teach.b: That's why a mantra is learned carefully, syllable by syllable, why chanting begins with Om, and why later tradition honors speech and learning as the goddess Saraswati.
Many who recite the Devi Mahatmya add this very hymn, the Devi Sukta.
Today: we spend words all day, in texts, comments, the thing said too fast. In this hymn, speech is not a tool we own; it is her.
Some teachers draw a plain lesson from it: treat your words as hers, on loan, and spend them with care. Tomorrow the path turns to a hymn sung to a goddess: the Sri Sukta.

how: This hymn, Rig Veda 10.125, is known as the Devi Sukta or Vak Sukta; it is chanted in goddess worship, and some recite it alongside the Devi Mahatmya.

games.q: what does “shakti as a philosophy” mean?
o: the divine power itself, speaking in the first person
a spell that gives a singer a beautiful voice
a hymn that praises the gods for their weapons

games.q: the goddess speaks — tap the pairs.
p: Mitra and Varuna, Indra and Agni

s: in this hymn, the gods hold the goddess up
she says she holds them up.
the hymn says people live in her without knowing it
through her they eat, see, breathe and hear, without knowing it.
this hymn is sung to the goddess by a priest
it is sung by her, in the first person, and tradition names her as its seer.

games.q: your cousin rushes through a mantra like a grocery list. by the Vak hymn, why do Hindus take care with sacred sound?
o: it doesn't matter how it's said; only the meaning counts.
speech is the goddess's power: the sound itself is sacred.
the gods get angry at mistakes and punish you.
games.why: in Rig Veda 10.125, Vak, speech herself, says everyone eats, sees, breathes and hears through her. sound is Shakti, so it's said with care.

practice: Let the breath come on its own, and notice it as the hymn does: something breathing through you, not only something you do.
Then add hearing, the sounds arriving without effort, and seeing, light on the eyelids or the room, and rest in all of it at once.
If you pray, you can hold the word Devi, or Ma, with the out-breath; if you don't, just rest in the breathing.

wordCard.voice: Shakti as a philosophy. In the Rig Veda, Vak speaks for herself: through her the world eats, sees, breathes and hears, and she breathes out like the wind.

orig.note: Sanskrit: vak, speech; the goddess who speaks Rig Veda 10.125 in her own voice.
